source_document.body:
Editor’s note: This is a contributed commentary. It comes amid FMCSA’s ongoing revocation of registered ELDs over hours-of-service log manipulation and FreightWaves welcomes responses from other parties.
An ELD connection has become an important part of how freight moves. Brokers use it to understand whether a carrier is operating, whether vehicles are associated with that carrier, and whether the right truck is present for a load. Carriers use that connection to demonstrate their capacity and gain access to freight.
That makes the integrity of the provider behind the connection consequential. A technical integration cannot be treated as a universal endorsement of everything that provider does. It has to be governed by standards, reviewed as conditions change, and subject to action when those standards fail.
Highway has worked with hundreds of ELD providers over nearly five years. We do not charge providers to integrate. FMCSA registration is a starting point, but it is not a blanket pass into Highway. We maintain our own requirements for integrations and the data they contribute. We can decline an integration or end one that does not meet those requirements, and we have ended integrations with providers that remained on FMCSA’s registered list. We also examine providers that reappear under a new name after a prior provider was revoked . A new label does not erase the underlying history.
None of this means every carrier using a problematic ELD provider is doing something wrong. A single provider may serve hundreds or thousands of legitimate businesses. If concerns arise, brokers need a clear view of risk and a way to act on it, while good carriers need a fair path to keep working. We can introduce appropriate controls around the carriers or transactions that present concern as we establish the facts. When an integration must end, we work to give legitimate carriers notice and a workable opportunity to change providers. Enforcement has to protect the network without treating every customer of a provider as guilty.
It is also important to be precise about what different data can establish. Highway does not receive drivers’ hours of service records through these integrations or perform the safety reviews assigned to FMCSA. Reports of manipulated logs warrant serious scrutiny. At the same time, ELD telemetry is one input in a broader assessment of carrier identity and cargo risk. It should never be asked to carry a decision by itself.
In nearly five years of operating Highway, we have not identified a successful cargo theft in which manipulated ELD data was relied on for a carrier hiring or tendering decision. That describes the losses we have investigated. It does not mean ELD manipulation is harmless or that providers should face no consequences for it. It means the industry should distinguish hours of service enforcement from the particular question of whether a cargo decision was defeated by falsified ELD data. Both deserve accurate evidence and appropriate action.
We are now building another layer of accountability through the Highway Certified Partner Network program. Participating providers, in multiple categories, will make additional commitments to the integrity and reliable delivery of the data they contribute. Brokers and carriers will be able to see which providers have made those commitments and make their own decisions accordingly. Participation in certification is voluntary. Meeting Highway’s existing requirements to maintain an integration is not. Certification creates a higher, visible standard; it does not replace enforcement of the baseline. This is not just about ELD providers. We started this with insurance agents and will extend that accountability requirement to anyone who contributes data to a freight transaction and hiring decision.

Meeting Highway’s existing requirements to maintain an integration is not. Certification creates a higher, visible standard; it does not replace enforcement of the baseline. This is not just about ELD providers. We started this with insurance agents and will extend that accountability requirement to anyone who contributes data to a freight transaction and hiring decision.
The real test of any standard is what happens when a transaction fails. Highway puts its own balance sheet behind qualifying loads with a Performance Guarantee of up to $100,000. Across roughly one million guaranteed loads, it has paid out once . We can make that commitment because the guarantee is tied to a broader, enforceable assessment of the carrier and the load, rather than a single signal from a single provider.
The freight market needs an ELD ecosystem in which a provider’s commitments are visible, its data can be trusted, and failures have consequences. Brokers should be able to set the bar for the freight they move. Legitimate carriers should have a fair path when their provider fails it. Highway will keep enforcing the standard and standing behind qualifying loads that meet it.
Questions will come. They should. But many of the loudest questions in this market come from pundits and competitors who attempt to demand an instant declaration without owning the consequences of that declaration. They are free to ask. They are not the people to whom Highway is accountable. We answer to the brokers and carriers who trust us with decisions that affect freight and livelihoods. We are their stewards, and we are proud of how we show up for them.
Theodore Roosevelt’s man in the arena comes to mind.
The arena in freight is a load at risk, a legitimate carrier trying to keep working, and a customer who needs someone to make a decision and own it. It is easy to call for a sweeping action from the stands. It is harder to establish the facts, apply a standard fairly, and remain accountable for what happens next. That is the work we have chosen.
We have yet to see another carrier identity platform pair an enforceable standard with a performance guarantee across this volume of freight, who “bear the brunt of the day”. We will welcome anyone willing to meet that bar. Until then, we are back in the arena doing the work, correcting course when the evidence calls for it, and putting our own balance sheet behind qualifying loads. Our customers deserve nothing less.
Michael Caney is Chief Commercial Officer of Highway, a carrier identity and fraud-prevention platform. Highway’s products, including its Certified Partner Network and Performance Guarantee, are discussed in this article. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect those of FreightWaves.
